idiom_name: repository class holding a Session, querying via session.scalars(select(...))
implementation_notes: SQLAlchemy's Session already provides the unit of work and the identity map, so the repository collapses to a thin object holding the Session and exposing domain-language methods that build select() statements; session.scalars(select(Invoice).where(...)) returns ORM entities and Session.add/delete are the collection operations. Type the boundary with a Protocol so tests can substitute an in-memory implementation, and leave commit to the unit of work. Many Python codebases skip the class and pass the Session to plain functions - the same realization with less ceremony, and equally valid.
pitfalls: Session is not thread-safe and must be one per unit of work; sharing it across threads or asyncio tasks (for example a FastAPI background task) produces inconsistent identity maps and stale reads.
Calling session.commit() inside a repository method commits half a business operation and expires loaded objects, so later attribute access triggers surprise reloads or DetachedInstanceError.
Returning Query/select() objects or leaking them to callers recreates the duplicate-query problem the repository was introduced to remove.

variants.name: No-ORM module over sqlite3 / DB-API returning dataclasses
variants.idiom_name: functions + dataclasses over the stdlib sqlite3 module
variants.implementation_notes: When the schema is small or SQL must stay explicit, the repository is a module of functions over sqlite3 (or psycopg) using execute plus fetchone/fetchall with row_factory = sqlite3.Row, returning frozen dataclasses as domain objects. This is the classic structure hand-written with the standard library: module functions are the collection interface, a from_row classmethod is the mapper, and transactions come from Connection context managers. Choose it when no ORM is present (scripts, embedded, small services) and when SQL reviewability beats mapping convenience.
pitfalls: With no ORM there is no identity map or change tracking: read-modify-write cycles must re-read and update explicitly, otherwise concurrent writers silently overwrite each other.
DB-API transaction behaviour is per connection and implicit; leave conn.commit() to the unit-of-work boundary and never commit inside a read helper, or readers will flush unrelated pending writes.
Parameterise every statement: f-string SQL is the standard injection foot-gun, and sqlite3 also needs detect_types/adapters set deliberately for dates and decimals.
